turns.text: Hi, Ishan. Can you hear me clearly?
Hi, Daniel. Yes, I can hear you. Is my audio okay?
It is. There was a brief delay when you joined, but it seems stable now. If it changes, we'll pause rather than talk over the connection.
Sounds good. Thank you.

We have about forty-five minutes. We'll spend most of it on a system-design problem. I care about requirements, tradeoffs, and failure behavior more than drawing every possible component. I'll redirect if we need to move on.
Yes, that works for me.
Before we get into the main round, could you give me a brief description of yourself and what you've been working on recently?

I'm a backend and platform engineer whose recent work includes secure object ingestion and metadata platforms in Java. I have designed event-driven and data-intensive services, operated them on call, and led bounded migrations. I have not built every feature in today's prompt at the exact stated scale, so I will use the requirements we establish rather than pretend my previous architecture transfers unchanged.
What architecture or operational decision in that work was specifically yours?

In my current work on secure object ingestion and metadata platforms in Java, I owned the service boundary, failure contract, and rollout metrics for one major change. A staff engineer reviewed the design, two engineers shared implementation, and another team owned the upstream producer. My decisions were the consistency boundary, the recovery behavior, and when staged traffic could advance.
Design secure file storage and sharing for business customers.
Who are the users, and which actions are in scope?

Users upload large files, organize folders, download, create revocable share links, manage permissions, and retain versions. Virus scanning and audit are required. Collaborative editing and content search are out of scope.
What scale, read-write shape, and latency should drive the design?

Five terabytes uploaded per day, files from bytes to fifty gigabytes, one hundred million stored files, read traffic four times write traffic, and customers in India, Europe, and North America. Metadata operations should usually be under two hundred milliseconds.
Which correctness, availability, or ordering promises matter most?

File bytes must be durable once upload completion succeeds. Permission revocation should take effect quickly. Multipart upload may resume. Downloads can use signed URLs but cannot bypass current authorization. Versions and deletion have explicit retention rules.
Should I include user-interface implementation, billing, and advanced analytics?
No. Define backend APIs and behavior, but exclude UI implementation, billing, and features not named in scope.
May I choose a home region or should every write be active-active globally?
Start with the simplest regional model that meets the requirement. Explain what would force you to add multi-region write complexity.
What retention, audit, and deletion behavior should I preserve?
Retain operational history long enough for customer support and audit. State a reasonable policy and separate reversible soft deletion from irreversible cleanup.

I'll design the core actions and contracts just named, optimize for the stated peak and quality priorities, and exclude the advanced features. I will identify the source of truth, one detailed write and read path, then test failures and regional behavior. The most important domain constraints appear to be: File bytes must be durable once upload completion succeeds. Permission revocation should take effect quickly. Multipart upload may resume. Downloads can use signed URLs but cannot bypass current authorization. Versions and deletion have explicit retention rules.
That scope is right. Go ahead.

Five terabytes per day becomes petabytes over years, so object storage lifecycle and deduplication economics matter more than storing bytes in a database. Metadata at a few hundred bytes per file is tens of gigabytes plus indexes, but folder and permission queries are latency-sensitive. Upload bandwidth and cross-region replication dominate infrastructure cost.
Which assumption in that estimate is weakest, and which decision would change if it is wrong?

The distribution tail is weaker than the average: hot tenants, large payloads, or fan-out can dominate even when aggregate volume looks manageable. I would measure the ninety-fifth and ninety-ninth percentiles and enforce explicit limits. The estimate supports separating high-volume immutable data from control metadata, but I would not purchase capacity or choose a partition count from one median number.
What correctness or product invariants are you protecting?

File bytes must be durable once upload completion succeeds. Permission revocation should take effect quickly. Multipart upload may resume. Downloads can use signed URLs but cannot bypass current authorization. Versions and deletion have explicit retention rules. I would also require idempotent client retries, an auditable state transition for every durable mutation, and bounded recovery so an outage cannot convert into a second overload incident.
Walk me through the high-level design.

A metadata service authenticates users, creates an upload session, and issues restricted multipart URLs to regional object storage. The client uploads parts directly, then completion verifies checksums and creates an immutable file version in a transaction with metadata. A scan pipeline quarantines new versions before normal sharing. Download requests authorize current permissions and issue short-lived signed URLs. Audit, retention, and replication consume events.
Where is the source of truth?

The authoritative control and user-visible state follows this model: File is a stable logical object with tenant, owner, folder, current version, and status. FileVersion has object key, size, checksum, encryption key reference, scan state, retention state, and creation time. ACL entries or group grants are versioned. ShareLink stores a random token hash, scope, expiry, and revoked time; upload sessions track parts and expiration. Caches, indexes, analytics, and queues are derived or transport layers; each needs a named freshness and rebuild path.
Walk one accepted write through the system.

The client receives part URLs bound to tenant, object key, size limits, and expiry, uploads directly, and submits part checksums. Completion validates storage state, writes the version and outbox, and returns a quarantined or processing status until scanning succeeds. Download always begins with metadata authorization; a cached signed URL is short enough that revocation exposure remains bounded.
Where do you need idempotency?

At the public mutation boundary, at every database-to-queue handoff, and at consumers that can repeat an external effect. I use a caller-scoped idempotency key or stable domain identifier, persist the result with the mutation, and make duplicates return the original outcome. Idempotency does not turn an ambiguous external timeout into exactly once; it only bounds effects we control.
You introduced several components. What would you remove from version one?

Use regional upload endpoints with one home metadata region per tenant, asynchronous cross-region durability, and short-lived download URLs. Avoid active-active metadata writes until a measured collaboration requirement justifies conflict handling.
I heard a technology reflex in that answer. Reconsider it.

Ishan initially proposes content-hash deduplication across all tenants, then drops cross-tenant dedup because it complicates privacy, deletion guarantees, and side-channel resistance; any dedup starts within a tenant. The correction is to restate the required capability first and select the simplest component the team can operate reliably.
How do you partition without creating a hot customer?

Use a high-cardinality stable key for the primary write path and retain tenant as an authorization and fairness dimension. Very large tenants can be promoted to dedicated shards or scheduling buckets. I would not make tenant ID the only physical partition key when the prompt explicitly permits one tenant to dominate traffic.
What changes at ten times scale?

I would first identify the measured bottleneck: edge bandwidth, hot metadata, queue lag, connection count, or background fan-out. Then scale that dimension through more partitions, regional reads, batching, or asynchronous work. I would not add multi-region consensus merely because the traffic number has another zero.
How do you turn the traffic estimate into an initial capacity plan?

I separate steady state, stated peak, and controlled recovery load. Stateless services can begin with enough replicas for roughly twice the normal peak while autoscaling on saturation and queue age, but stateful partitions require measured item size, write amplification, replication, and hot-key headroom. I would load-test the dominant path and set an explicit admission limit before launch. Capacity without a rejection or backpressure policy is only an optimistic chart. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the metadata and blobs boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What is your consistency model from the user's perspective?

Authoritative mutations use conditional or transactional writes in the home ownership boundary. Derived caches, indexes, analytics, and regional replicas are eventually consistent with a stated objective. For each stale read I name the user consequence and whether the system may serve stale, fail closed, or bypass the cache. Security revocation and destructive state receive a tighter propagation path than ordinary analytics freshness. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the uploads boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How do schema changes remain compatible during a rolling deployment?

Use versioned contracts and expand-migrate-contract: add fields or readers first, keep old writers valid, backfill or dual-read with measurable comparison, move writers, then remove the old form only after usage reaches zero. Consumers ignore unknown additive fields where safe. A breaking semantic change receives a new version rather than reusing the same field name with a different meaning. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the permissions boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What lifecycle applies to the largest or fastest-growing data?

Classify data by operational need, support window, audit, and legal retention. Hot state stays queryable; immutable payloads or history move to cheaper storage with indexes for bounded retrieval; expired derivatives can be rebuilt or deleted. Deletion is a workflow with tombstone, asynchronous cleanup, verification, and legal-hold checks. I would track bytes by tenant and class so retention policy has a measurable cost. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the versioning boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How do you test correctness beyond unit tests?

Use contract tests at API and event boundaries, deterministic fault injection for timeout and duplicate delivery, replay of representative production shapes with sensitive data removed, and invariant checks on sampled state. Staging should test recovery from partial completion, not only happy-path throughput. Before launch I would run a game day for the failure that creates the most ambiguous external or customer-visible state. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the multi-region boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How would you control infrastructure cost without hiding product risk?

Measure cost per successful user outcome, not only per request. The largest levers are retention, replication, egress, fan-out, cache efficiency, and retry amplification. I would set budgets and alert on trend, then change compression, lifecycle, batching, or tiering with correctness guardrails. Removing redundancy or shortening audit retention purely to hit a bill target requires an explicit product and risk decision. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the metadata and blobs boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What does a safe migration from an existing system look like?

Inventory callers and data ownership, define compatibility, then use shadow reads or dual calculations where results can be compared. Backfill is partitioned and resumable, with rate limits so it cannot starve normal traffic. Cut over by low-risk tenant or region, retain a bounded rollback path, and stop dual behavior after evidence and a deadline; permanent dual writes create a second source of truth. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the uploads boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
If one partition becomes hot, how do you detect and repair it?

Observe per-partition throughput, latency, queue age, key distribution, and throttling. Short-term mitigation can isolate or rate-limit the hot key, increase cache or consumer capacity, and protect other shards. Durable repair may split by a secondary hash, promote a large tenant, or change a fan-out model. Repartitioning needs a versioned routing map and gradual movement so clients do not guess ownership. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the permissions boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What changes if the home region is unavailable for several hours?

Read-only or bounded-stale operations can fail over to a replica if the product accepts the state. For writes, promote only after fencing the old region and confirming the recovery point; otherwise two authorities can diverge. Queue new work durably where possible and expose delayed state. When the region returns, reconcile from versioned logs and drain deliberately instead of replaying every operation at full speed. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the versioning boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How do privacy and data minimization affect observability?

Carry stable opaque identifiers rather than payloads, redact credentials and content at the logging library, limit tenant-level access, and retain detailed traces for a bounded window. Metrics use low-cardinality dimensions; high-cardinality investigation moves to indexed logs with access audit. Sampling must preserve errors and rare security states. Debuggability is a requirement, but collecting every customer field is not the only way to achieve it. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the multi-region boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What SLO would you publish, and what happens when it is missed?

Publish the user-visible latency, availability, or freshness objective that matches the core path, plus a correctness indicator that is not hidden by fast failures. Error-budget burn triggers a response proportional to rate and duration: investigate, pause risky rollout, or shift capacity. The SLO should influence prioritization; if misses create only a dashboard color, it is not operating the system. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the metadata and blobs boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
What belongs in the support runbook?

Start from the customer's symptom and safe identifiers, then list current state, expected delay, common response categories, containment steps, escalation owner, and actions support must not take. Repair or replay commands are audited and idempotent. The runbook says when an outcome is ambiguous and what to tell the customer; it does not require support to infer semantics from internal service names. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the uploads boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
How would you review this design with teams in three time zones?

Post a concise proposal with requirements, invariants, diagram, rejected options, failure behavior, and open decisions. Every question gets an owner and deadline, and one named decider closes it. Use overlap for the few tradeoffs that cannot converge asynchronously, then update the written record immediately. Quiet is not treated as agreement when a team owns a critical dependency; their review is explicitly requested. For this design, I would verify it specifically at the permissions boundary rather than assume the generic rule is enough.
Give me the minimum useful data model.

File is a stable logical object with tenant, owner, folder, current version, and status. FileVersion has object key, size, checksum, encryption key reference, scan state, retention state, and creation time. ACL entries or group grants are versioned. ShareLink stores a random token hash, scope, expiry, and revoked time; upload sessions track parts and expiration.
Which APIs define the product contract?

POST /files/uploads creates a session with expected size and checksum policy; POST completion commits a version idempotently; GET /files/{id}/download authorizes and returns a short-lived URL; permission and share-link APIs use versions to prevent lost updates; DELETE applies soft-delete and retention policy rather than immediately removing bytes.
How do you prevent a database write followed by a failed queue publish from losing work?

Write an outbox record in the same transaction as the authoritative mutation. A publisher sends it at least once and marks progress. Consumers deduplicate using the stable entity or event ID. If the chosen data store lacks multi-record transactions, co-locate the state and outbox in one atomic item or use a durable log as the source rather than hand-wave a cross-system transaction.
What data belongs outside the primary control store?

Large immutable bytes, append-only raw events, search indexes, and analytics aggregates should use stores suited to those access patterns. The primary control store retains identifiers, ownership, versions, state, and references. Separation reduces cost and hot-row pressure, but each external object needs lifecycle and consistency rules so metadata cannot point forever at missing content.
How are concurrent updates handled?

Use version numbers or conditional writes for user-visible mutable state. A stale client receives a conflict and refreshes rather than overwriting a newer decision. For workflows, state transitions are explicit and monotonic where possible; background workers carry the version or fencing token they claimed.
What would you cache?

Cache only read-heavy values with a clear invalidation or bounded-staleness rule. Include entity version in the cached value, use jittered TTLs, and protect misses with request coalescing. Security revocation and destructive state usually need shorter TTLs or an active invalidation path than ordinary immutable content.
Pressure-test the design against orphaned multipart uploads. What happens and how does it recover?

For orphaned multipart uploads, I first preserve the source-of-truth invariant and prevent unbounded retry. The system records an explicit degraded state, uses deadlines, backoff, jitter, and idempotent transitions, and exposes the condition through user-impact metrics. Recovery is controlled rather than releasing the whole backlog at once. For this design specifically, the affected component follows the ownership boundary already described, and any ambiguous external effect remains visible rather than being relabeled success.

How do you protect healthy tenants while recovering a backlog?

Separate new work from retries, reserve capacity for the normal path, and apply tenant and endpoint admission controls. Recovery drains by oldest age and priority while watching saturation and downstream success. A large failed tenant cannot consume every worker merely because its queue is deepest.
What is the disaster-recovery posture?

Start with replicated durable data and a tested regional failover procedure. If the design uses a home write region, failover requires a fencing or promotion decision before writes resume elsewhere. Read paths may fail over sooner if bounded staleness is acceptable. Define recovery-time and recovery-point objectives rather than claiming instant lossless failover.
Give me the highest-risk security controls.

Tenant-isolated authorization, envelope encryption with managed keys, malware quarantine, content-type and size validation, private object buckets, short-lived signed URLs, token hashes for share links, audit of access and permission changes, and restricted service identities. I would threat-model the public or cross-tenant boundary and make authorization part of the normal data path, not a gateway-only assumption.
What would you alert on?

Upload success and resume rate, completion latency, orphaned part bytes, scan backlog age, download authorization failures, signed-URL issuance, replication lag, checksum mismatches, revocation propagation, and retention deletion errors. Alerts should connect to user impact or exhaustion trends; dashboards alone are not an operating mechanism.
How does support trace one customer's report?

Expose a safe request, entity, and attempt identifier to the customer. Carry it through logs, queue messages, traces, and state history. Support can retrieve status without viewing sensitive payloads, while operators can pivot by region, shard, response category, and version.
How would you roll out the riskiest change?

Use shadow reads or dual writes only where their comparison semantics are clear, then canary by tenant and region with automated rollback thresholds. Validate recovery, not only success. Keep old readers compatible until the migration checkpoint proves they are no longer needed.
Give me a short recap and name the tradeoff you would expect me to challenge.

Large bytes flow directly to object storage while a strongly controlled metadata plane owns identity, versions, permissions, and retention. Completion is idempotent and scanning gates availability; every download reauthorizes before issuing a short-lived URL. The main tradeoff is regional performance versus metadata consistency, so the first version uses tenant home regions and bounded replication rather than active-active permission writes.
I have what I need. What questions do you have for me?
Which part of this system is hardest for the team in production today?
Permission revocation, retention, and partial upload cleanup are harder than storing the bytes.
That aligns with the failure cases we discussed.
How are design decisions reviewed across time zones?
The author posts a short proposal with a deadline and named decider. Most comments are asynchronous; unresolved tradeoffs get a focused overlap call and a written decision afterward.
That is the working model I'm looking for.
Those were my main questions. Thank you for the context and for your time.
I need to finish my notes and compare them with the rest of the interview team, so I won't give feedback on this call. The recruiter will contact you about the next step within a few business days.
Understood. Thank you, Daniel. Have a good day.
You too, Ishan. Take care.
